charts.title: Gross Profit, Operating Income & Net Income
Revenue by Segment
charts.annotation: Stacked by segment, FY2019 onward. Brakes drops from ~¥178.5bn (FY2023) to ~¥58.2bn (FY2024) when the TMD Friction divestiture closed in Nov 2023 — not an operating decline.

charts.title: Operating Profit by Segment
charts.annotation: Several segments swing between profit and loss year to year (e.g. Brakes, MicroDevices) — group operating income is not a smooth blend of seven businesses.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by segment
segmentRevenue.content:
Nisshinbo reports seven segments: Wireless (automotive/industrial wireless modules and radio products -- the largest and fastest-growing segment), MicroDevices (semiconductors, including New JRC analog/power ICs), Brakes (brake materials and components), Precision Instruments (precision machinery, bearings, motors), Chemicals (specialty chemicals, airbag inflators), Textiles (the legacy spinning/weaving business) and Real Estate (property leasing and development on former mill sites).

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the Brakes segment's revenue collapses from roughly ¥178.5bn in FY2023 to roughly ¥58.2bn in FY2024 because the TMD Friction subsidiary (the group's European/global brake-friction business) was divested, closing in November 2023 -- that is a portfolio change, not a demand collapse, and the DCF's growth assumptions should be read with it in mind.

What to watch:

  • Wireless's rising share of group revenue (it overtook all other segments combined by FY2024-FY2025)
  • Textiles' slow structural decline
  • Any further divestitures changing segment composition, as TMD Friction did

segmentOperatingProfit.title: Operating profit by segment
segmentOperatingProfit.content:
The same seven segments' contribution to group operating profit -- revenue share does not translate directly into profit share for a conglomerate this diversified.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: Brakes and MicroDevices have both swung from meaningful profit to loss and back within a few years (MicroDevices: profit in FY2021-FY2022, a ¥7.1bn loss in FY2024), so group operating income is the net of volatile, sometimes offsetting segment results rather than a smooth blend. Chemicals turned from consistent profit to a small loss by FY2025.

What to watch:

  • Whether Wireless's growing revenue share is converting into a growing profit share
  • Segments swinging to loss in the same year (correlated cyclicality vs. idiosyncratic problems)
  • Real Estate as the structurally steady, if small, profit contributor

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Nisshinbo Holdings Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
